description:
Introducing Team Los Pollos Cosmicos! 🚀
Based in Baku, we are tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. We engineered Project AETHRA — a high-precision lunar mission planning workstation for Artemis & CLPS South Pole sites. Our tool calculates solar illumination angles, DSN comms windows, horizon profiles, and slope hazard analytics to evaluate landing safety and mission feasibility. Open to collaborators. Let's make history! 🌕
summary:
Aethra is an open-source geographic information system (GIS) and orbital analysis interface designed to evaluate candidate landing sites for the NASA Artemis and Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) missions. At polar lunar latitudes, low solar elevation angles (sub-2 degrees) create dynamic terrain shadows, while polar libration causes periodic loss of line-of-sight to Earth's Deep Space Network (DSN) stations. 

Aethra resolves these constraints by integrating NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) 80-meter and 5-meter digital elevation models with planetary ephemeris data across 14-day mission windows at 30-minute intervals. The system computes 360-degree radial horizon masks up to 140 km from each target to assess line-of-sight occultation. Using a Multi-Attribute Decision Analysis (MADA) framework aligned with NASA/SP-2016-6105 guidelines, Aethra scores sites across lander survival duration (40%), direct Earth communication (30%), solar power collection (20%), and terrain slope safety (10%). All computations and 3D WebGL visualisations execute entirely client-side with zero server latency.
details:
System Architecture and Operation:

Aethra operates as a zero-latency client-side WebGIS application developed with React 19, Vite, and Three.js. Topographic data from NASA's Planetary Data System is pre-processed into packed binary float height arrays (.bin) containing 65,536 elevation vertices per target region. These vertices are dynamically loaded and rendered in WebGL vertex shaders at 60 frames per second, allowing interactive orbit, rotation, and elevation exaggeration (1.0x to 4.0x).

Computational Methodology:

1. Topographic Horizon Masking: For each candidate site, apparent horizon elevations are calculated along 360 azimuth rays up to 140 km from the center, accounting for spherical lunar curvature (R_Moon = 1,737.4 km). Local 5 m DEMs refine near-field ridge geometry where available.

2. Ephemeris and Geometry: Topocentric elevation and azimuth angles of the Sun and Earth are computed at 30-minute steps across a 14-day lunar daylight cycle. Direct line of sight exists when the celestial body's elevation exceeds the local horizon mask angle.

3. Subsystem Balances: The lander model simulates a 500 W vertical cylindrical solar array, an 80 W baseline avionics load, survival heating during shadowing, and a 1.5 kWh Li-ion battery bank. A site is classified as NO-GO if cumulative shadows deplete the battery reserve below 0%.

Site Evaluation Findings:

Across the five evaluated candidate zones, Malapert Massif (Site 23, 85.99°S, 0.24°W, elevation +4,780 m) achieved the highest composite rating (98/100). Its elevated plateau provides 100% continuous direct-to-Earth line of sight across polar libration cycles, eliminating relay satellite requirements, combined with extended solar visibility periods.

Software Stack and Verification:

- Languages and Frameworks: JavaScript (ES6+), React 19, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, Astronomy Engine.

- Data Validation: Horizon profiles calculated from regional 80 m DEMs were cross-validated against 5 m local DEMs within a 5 km operational radius, confirming a mean angular difference of < 1.50 degrees.

- License: Fully open-source under the MIT License.
